newsitem.title: USA: NASD fines N.Y. firm, executives more than $5 million.
newsitem.headline: NASD fines N.Y. firm, executives more than $5 million.

text.p: The National Association of Securities Dealers said Thursday it fined a New York brokerage and its former principal more than $5 million for alleged stock manipulation and other fair trade practice violations.
The NASD said it imposed a $5 million fine against Lawrence Rosenberg, former chief executive officer of Duke & Co., and barred him from asociation with any NASD member in any capacity.
As a result of the scheme, the NASD's market regulation committee alleged that victims suffered an estimated $3.5 million in losses and that Rosenberg and others made about $2.8 million in profits.
The fine against Rosenberg is one of the biggest imposed by NASD against a brokerage executive, an NASD spokesman. NASD is the self-regulatory organization for the nation's brokerage industry.

The NASD's Market Regulation Committee, which instituted the proceedings, accepted a settlement offer by the brokerage and Salvatore Saporito, the firm's head trader. Saporito and the brokerage were named in an original complaint filed in February 1996 against Duke.
Without admitting or denying any wrongdoing, Duke agreed to pay a $25,000 fine and to implement supervisory procedures to prevent recurrence of the alleged violations.
Saporito was fined $25,000 and was suspended from the brokerage industry for six months.
The company and Saporito did not return calls for comment. Rosenberg could not be reached.

Rosenberg, who was Duke's chief executive officer at the time of the alleged wrongdoing, was named respondent in an amended complaint in April 1996. The NASD said he denied the allegations but failed to appear in a Jan. 15 hearing.

The NASD said Rosenberg's licenses were revoked on August 17, 1995, for nonpayment of a fine the NASD imposed for his failure to provide testimony in connection with the trading of Hillside Bedding Inc.
According the NASD, Duke, through Saporito and Rosenberg, manipulated trading in the stock of Hillside Bedding a New York area retailer that went public in February 1993.
The lead underwriter in the initial public stock offering of the company was Elliot Allen & Co., which later became Duke. Rosenberg was president of Elliott at the time, NASD said.
The NASD alleged that Duke, acting through Rosenberg and Saporito, actively bid for and bought securities of Hillside while Duke was also acting as broker in the distrubtion of the company's stock.
As a result, between July 19 through August 2, 1993, the price of Hillside's stock rose from $4 to more than $9 a share, the NASD said.

The NASD committee found that Rosenberg played a pivotal role in directing this scheme, including manipulating the price, coordinating trades for three entities, with which Duke had a closer relationship, and sharing in the profits of those entities.

The panel estimated that Duke retail customers suffered a loss of about $3.5 million as a result of the manipulation and that Rosenberg and others in the scheme made more than $2.8 million in profits from the sales by the three entities.
